title: Rocky Planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars

cards.b: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars formed from the same cloud, close to the Sun. Yet one is scorched, one is a greenhouse oven, one is alive and one is a frozen desert. Comparing them is how we learn what keeps a planet habitable, a question that matters for our own future and for exoplanets.

The inner planets are small and dense, made of rock and metal with thin or no atmospheres. Each has a metal core, a rocky mantle and a crust. They are called terrestrial planets. They formed near the Sun where only rock and metal could stay solid, while lighter gases were blown outward.

Mercury is only 38 percent of Earth's width, with almost no atmosphere. It circles the Sun in 88 days but spins slowly: three spins in two orbits, so a day from sunrise to sunrise lasts 176 Earth days. Temperatures swing from about 430 C in daylight to -180 C at night. Craters at its poles hold water ice in permanent shadow.

Venus is nearly Earth's twin in size, yet its thick carbon-dioxide atmosphere (about 90 times Earth's pressure) traps heat: surface 465 C, hotter than Mercury. Sulphuric-acid clouds cover it. It spins backward and so slowly (243 days) that its day is longer than its year (225 days). Early Venus may have had oceans; a runaway greenhouse boiled them away.

Earth sits in the Sun's habitable zone, where water can be liquid. Other helpers: a magnetic field from its liquid iron core that deflects the solar wind, plate tectonics that recycle carbon and regulate climate, a large Moon that stabilises the axis tilt, and a moderate atmosphere with a greenhouse effect, a gentle one, that keeps the average at about 15 C.

Mars is half Earth's width with 38 percent of Earth's gravity and a thin CO2 atmosphere under 1 percent of Earth's pressure. It has the Solar System's tallest volcano, Olympus Mons (about 22 km), and a canyon system, Valles Marineris, about 4,000 km long. Dry river valleys and minerals show it once had lots of liquid water, 3-4 billion years ago. Its small core cooled, the magnetic field faded, and the solar wind stripped most of its air.

Mars: Viking landers (1976), then rovers: Curiosity (2012) found ancient lake-bed rock, and Perseverance (landed 18 February 2021) is caching samples in Jezero crater, an ancient river delta. Venus: Soviet Venera landers survived minutes on its surface in the 1970s; Magellan radar-mapped it (1990s). Mercury: NASA's MESSENGER (2011-2015) and the ESA-JAXA BepiColombo mission under way.

• 'Mercury is the hottest planet.' Venus is hotter, due to its greenhouse effect.
  • 'Mars had canals.' Percival Lowell's 1890s 'canals' were optical illusions.
  • 'Greenhouse effect is bad in itself.' Without it Earth would average about -18 C. Too much is the problem, as Venus shows.

ISRO's Mars Orbiter Mission (Mangalyaan) launched on PSLV on 5 November 2013 and entered Mars orbit on 24 September 2014, making India the first country to reach Mars orbit on its first attempt, at a cost near Rs 450 crore. Its Mars Colour Camera imaged the whole planet. It worked for about eight years. India has approved a Venus Orbiter Mission (Shukrayaan), planned around 2028.

cards.h: Escape speed: Earth and Mars compared
cards.b:
To leave a planet for good you need an escape speed. It depends on the planet's mass and radius. Heavier and more compact planets hold on more tightly, and that decides which gases a planet can keep for billions of years.

Worked example, Earth. G times Earth's mass is about 3.99 x 10 to the power 14, and Earth's radius is 6.37 x 10 to the power 6 metres.
Step 1: 2 x 3.99 x 10 to the power 14 = 7.98 x 10 to the power 14.
Step 2: divide by 6.37 x 10 to the power 6: 1.25 x 10 to the power 8.
Step 3: take the square root: about 11,200 metres per second, or 11.2 km per second.

Worked example, Mars. G times Mars's mass is about 4.28 x 10 to the power 13, and its radius is 3.39 x 10 to the power 6 metres. The same steps give about 5.0 km per second, less than half of Earth's.

Here v is the escape speed in metres per second, G the gravitational constant, M the planet's mass in kilograms and R its radius in metres: v = square root of (2 x G x M / R).

Exam trap: escape speed does not depend on the mass of the object leaving. A rocket and a feather need the same speed to leave, ignoring air.

• Terrestrial planets are small, rocky, with metal cores.
  • Venus is the hottest, from a runaway greenhouse effect.
  • Earth's life-friendly traits: water, magnetic field, tectonics, stable tilt.
  • Mars once had water but lost its air and field.

Think about it: (1) What does Venus warn us about greenhouse gases? (2) Why might small planets lose their atmospheres sooner?

quiz.q: Why does Venus's day outlast its year?
o: It spins very slowly (243 d) while orbiting in 225 d

quiz.q: Mars has a thin atmosphere mainly because:
o: Solar wind stripped it after its field faded
Gas froze at the poles only
It is too close to Sun
quiz.w: Weak gravity and no magnetic shield.

o: The tallest known volcano in the Solar System

quiz.q: Earth's average temperature without any greenhouse effect would be about:
quiz.w: Greenhouse effect raises it by around 33 C.

quiz.q: India's Mars Orbiter Mission reached Mars orbit on:
Which planet's magnetic field shields it from the solar wind and comes from a liquid core?
Why does Mercury, with no air, have such extreme temperature swings?
quiz.w: No air to spread or trap heat.

quiz.q: Evidence that Mars once had water includes:
o: Dry river valleys and lake-bed rocks

quiz.q: Terrestrial planets formed close to the Sun because:
o: Only rock and metal stayed solid there
